back: A place exposed to two or more different hazards, which may interact or follow one another, so that risk and the demands on response and recovery are higher.
Cascading: one hazard triggers another (rain on ash makes lahars). Compound: hazards occur together and their effects combine (Pinatubo and Typhoon Yunya).
Plate convergence in the Philippine Mobile Belt (Manila and Philippine Trenches, Philippine Fault) causes earthquakes and volcanoes; the warm western Pacific produces typhoons.
Luzon earthquake 1990 (magnitude 7.7, about 1 600 deaths); Pinatubo 1991 (about 800 deaths); Bohol 2013 (magnitude 7.2, over 200 deaths); Haiyan 2013 (over 6 000 deaths); Taal 2020.
PAGASA: weather and typhoons. PHIVOLCS: earthquakes and volcanoes. Republic Act 10121 (2010): shift from relief to risk reduction, with local plans and funds.
Strengths: monitoring, warnings, drills and a strong law. Limits: informal housing in hazard zones, weak code enforcement, gaps in warnings (Haiyan) and repeated hazards.

front: Why people stay in hazard zones
back: Fertile soils, fishing, jobs, poverty and lack of alternatives, family ties, and underestimating rare events.
